rows.text: Police intervention after student clashes; Army breached San Ildefonso school door with bazooka early July 30
CNH constituted with three assembly-elected delegates per striking school and no political-party delegation
Six demands include release of political prisoners, end to granaderos, repeal of Penal Code 145/145 bis, reparations and accountability
UNAM retrospective estimates 100,000 on Zacatenco–Casco Santo Tomás march; participants proposed 72-hour ultimatum
March from Anthropology Museum to Zócalo; El Día's estimate of 400,000 is not verified headcount
UNAM lists UNAM/IPN/Chapingo student speakers, teachers, worker and mother; letter from jailed railroad leader read
Student participants allegedly obtained ecclesiastical permission to ring Cathedral bells
CNH speaker publicly proposed broadcast government talks in Zócalo on Sept 1; proposal not outcome
Predawn forces cleared Zócalo campers; UNAM reconstructs nearby pursuit through Madero, 5 de Mayo, 16 de Septiembre
UNAM reports solidarity strike by 220 medical trainees at Hospital General
CNH proposed public broadcast IMSS Centro Médico talks; campaign target one million signatures, not actual total
Army occupied Ciudad Universitaria and Rector Barros Sierra condemned action next day; UNAM reports detentions including Ifigenia Martínez
Radio UNAM preserves 17 reels of student-produced news; archived audio not personally heard
UNAM retrospective reports rally of approximately 5,000 at Tlatelolco; fatality and injury totals remain unresolved
UNAM inaugurated Monumento a la Ausencia at CCUT, with archival victim categorization (dead, injured, detained, disappeared)

On 24 February 1822 the First Constituent Congress convened in the former church of San Pedro y San Pablo; on 21 May Iturbide took the oath there as emperor, while the coronation was held at the Cathedral.

UNAM locates the Second Constituent Congress and the 4 October 1824 federal constitution promulgation at San Pedro y San Pablo; the legislature remained there until the 1829 move to the National Palace.

The 1856 Lerdo Law directed that certain corporate properties rented to tenants be adjudicated at a capital value derived from annual rent calculated at 6 percent; unleased eligible properties went to auction. These are provisions of law, not proof of individual implementation.

The 1856 law applied to civil corporations including municipalities and schools, but article 8 exempted institutional direct-use buildings and municipal lands devoted exclusively to public services. It did not itself command universal demolition of convents.

On 26 July 1856 Bishop Clemente de Jesús Munguía protested the Lerdo Law as forced sales to specified buyers and argued Church property rights were independent of state authorization; this documents his partisan position, not the truth of his legal contention.

On 12 July 1859 the Juárez government decreed that property administered by regular and secular clergy would enter the national domain and declared institutional separation of state and church. Its legal mechanism was distinct from the 1856 tenant-adjudication regime.

The 1859 law assigned sacred vessels, liturgical vestments and images of suppressed orders to diocesan bishops under formal inventory while directing manuscripts, books, paintings and antiquities to public collections. Actual transfer of any particular object still requires separate evidence.

The nationalization law suppressed male regular orders but permitted existing women's convents to continue. Exclaustrated nuns were to recover their dowries; mendicant nuns without dowries were promised 500 pesos. The later 1863 expulsion was a distinct measure.

Maximilian's decree of 26 February 1865 ordered review of transactions under the 1856 and 1859 laws, confirmed those made legally and authorized invalidation or rehabilitation of others, with certain latter cases subject to a 25 percent payment.

Article 9 of the 1865 imperial review decree rejected certain renunciations by women owning no other real property and by guardians on behalf of minors. This is a statutory restriction; actual enforcement has not been researched.

INAH reports that the Reforma-era division of the San Francisco complex opened the street connections associated with present-day Gante and 16 de Septiembre; former convent spaces were later used for a circus, stables, hotel and Protestant worship.

UNAM traces the former church's use as a military college in 1858–1860, later school/hospital/warehouse uses, its 1920–21 restoration and murals, and its role as National Newspaper Library from 1944 through 1979.

Juárez's 4 December 1860 law protected Catholic worship and other religions, conditioned practice on the rights of others and public order, treated religious membership as voluntary, and removed civil sanctions for purely religious offenses such as apostasy or heresy.

The 1860 law abolished church sanctuary and permitted secular authorities to apprehend accused persons in temples under ordinary law without ecclesiastical control over their access; a rule, not evidence of a specific arrest.
The 1860 law replaced obligatory religious oaths for officials, professions, testimony and certain declarations with explicit promises carrying legal consequences.

The 1860 law required local political authorities' written permission for each solemn religious act outside temples and allowed permits to be withheld or activities stopped when disorder threatened; it does not establish any particular procession was banned.

The 1860 law recognized freedom of religious marriage practice but assigned the marriage contract and its civil legal effects exclusively to secular law; lack of civil formalities prevented recognized civil effects.
Governors were instructed to enforce cemetery laws and guarantee dignified burial even if religious authorities refused religious services; no local enforcement outcomes were inspected.
The 1860 law preserved individual religious freedom for public officials but barred their attendance in an official capacity at worship events, including formed troops.

Juárez's 1861 decree secularized church-administered hospitals and charities, transferring direction and maintenance in the Federal District to the Union government and state establishments to oversight by the states. It does not prove any named hospital's implementation.

The 1861 hospital decree kept estates, revenues and capital dedicated to the welfare establishments, preserved prior lawful property measures and regulated voluntary redemption/reinvestment of capital rather than simply ordering immediate liquidation.
